summary: This RFC describes a Telnet option for avoiding a double login. It is meant mainly for connections made by terminal access controllers on behalf of users, but any two hosts can use it. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: TUID lets a Telnet connection carry a user's identifier after the two sides agree to the option. The receiving host can choose whether to accept the earlier authentication.

what is the tacacs user identification telnet option
what is the telnet tuid option
how does telnet avoid double login
subtitle: A Telnet option for passing an authenticated user's identifier to another host.

tldr.problem: A TACACS user may authenticate to a terminal access controller and then face another login at the target host.
tldr.mechanism: After both Telnet sides agree to TUID, the user side sends the user's 32-bit UUID in a subnegotiation.
tldr.outcome: A host may accept or decline the TAC's authentication; the memo requests discussion of the proposed protocol.

today: RFC 927 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Avoiding a Second Login
sections.content:
Under the TAC Access Control System (TACACS), a user authenticates to a terminal access controller before connecting through it to another host. To avoid asking the user to authenticate again, the controller can pass the user's proven identity, represented by a UUID, to the target host.

The target host may accept or reject that authentication. The option is intended mainly for TAC connections but may be used by any two consenting hosts.
sections.plainLanguage: The first system can send the user's identifier to the next host. That host decides whether to accept the earlier authentication.

sections.title: TUID Negotiation
sections.content:
The Telnet option is named TUID and has code 26. The server can send IAC DO TUID to request the identifier; the user side can answer IAC WILL TUID to agree or IAC WON'T TUID to refuse. The user side may also offer with WILL, and the server can accept with DO.

If a host does not implement the option, the default response is WON'T on the user side or DON'T on the server side. The UUID is sent only when both sides agree.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides must agree before the user identifier is sent. A side that does not support TUID refuses the negotiation.

sections.title: UUID Subnegotiation
sections.content:
The user Telnet sends IAC SB TUID <uuid> IAC SE. The UUID is a 32-bit binary number. The RFC's examples show the value 1 as four octets 0 0 0 1; Telnet's IAC byte is doubled when it appears within the value.

The memo describes two successful negotiation orders and two refusals. It is a proposed protocol for the ARPA-Internet community and asks for discussion and suggestions.
sections.plainLanguage: Once both sides agree, the user side sends the 32-bit identifier in a Telnet subnegotiation. The RFC also shows how a command byte inside the value is escaped.
